name: Morocco
lede: Morocco is the color of a leather, a deep brown in the library but a brick red in the one glossary that explains the word, and it is named for a country the color books mostly visit for other reasons.

sections.title: A leather before a color
sections.body:
St Clair's glossary of color names defines *morocco* as a brick red that was originally the color of painted leather [1]. The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 records the word as a color from 1919, on plate 8 [2]. How the leather was made and why it carried the country's name is not traced in the books we hold, so we do not say.

Literature gives one clear picture of it. In Mérimée's novella *Carmen*, of 1845, the heroine wears a very short red skirt and small red morocco shoes with a flame-colored ribbon [3]. Her dress is meant to shock the hero, and in Greenfield's account the red does most of the work [3]. Paterson's dictionary lists only the adjective *Moroccan*, for colors coming, or supposed to come, from the country [4].

sections.title: Brick red or dark brown
sections.body:
The swatch is not the brick red of the glossary. It is a very dark brown, close to the ISCC-NBS block called dark brown, at a distance of 4.9 units [2][5]. Redder versions exist as a separate name, [[morocco-red]] [5]. The nearest names to this brown are [[armada]], [[bistre]] and [[mahogany-brown]], the last a little redder [5].

So the word can mean a leather in a brick-red dye, as in St Clair, or a dark leather brown, as in this library [1][2]. Treat the swatch as a screen approximation of the second.

sections.title: The country, not the color
sections.body:
The color books mention the country mostly for its dyes and minerals. Balfour-Paul follows the indigo crop west through north Africa to the Draa valley, in the country's south [6]. Berber shawls striped in indigo and black were valued by the share of true indigo against the other black [7]. Dyers in the High Atlas believed that telling outrageous lies could revive a vat that had stopped working [8][9].

The *Pigment Compendium* names Moroccan sources for several mineral colors: malachite at Oujda, brochantite and vanadinite at Touissit, and erythrite at Bou Azzer [10].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color this dark brown is everywhere: it appears in 5,111 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 21.49 per cent, as photographed, and the within-painting lens finds it in 3,971 [11]. It is more common than 99 per cent of the named colors [11]. Its peak is the 1600s, at 21.6 per cent of the 6,394 paintings from that century, 1.2 times the baseline of the same museums [11].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, by lightness rank, in 43 per cent of the 3,971 [11]. The most devoted painter is [[painter:otto-van-veen|Otto van Veen]], in 11 of his 15 works here, 3.5 times the baseline [11]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not proof of leather, dye or pigment [11].
